beats.say: Count the five places on this Cambridge envelope. Prompt A asks for a number. Its copy starts with a two. Prompt B asks for all five digits. Line up the copies with the address. The grader reads the ZIP as a number. Which copies earn a point?
Both earn a point. The missing zero leaves the numeric value unchanged. The mailing label needs all five characters. Keep both copies and switch to exact text. How would you score them now?
Only B earns a point. Look straight down from the zero on the envelope. The empty place on A costs it the match. A prompt search rewards whatever the grader counts.

title: What comes back from the predictor?

beats.say: Now try a deployment question with DSPy, a library for building language model programs. Our examples use version three point four point zero. An engineer asks to deploy payment-service. The only admitted record allows a rollback of payment-tests. The signature declares the inputs, question and evidence, and asks for two output fields, route and record ID. The reviewed answer is abstain, with an empty ID.

The module calls the predictor. Its instruction says when to cite a record. A demonstration shows a worked answer, like the approved rollback. DSPy can compile a new prompt by changing the instruction or the examples. The host still checks the proposed action against its authorization policy.

Score the rollback first. Its label calls for serve and record forty-four twelve. The assistant gets the route right but cites record ninety-nine ninety-nine. Our grader compares the two fields to the reviewed label. How many points should this reply get?

Zero points. The route agrees, but the records differ. Put the approved ID back. Both fields now match, earning one point. Leave that point on the rollback. Now keep the reply and ask about deployment instead. The reviewed answer changes to abstain with an empty ID. The same reply earns zero.
The assistant cited the same real approval both times. It only supports the rollback. If a task allows several valid records, give the grader that approved set. A good grader needs good labels.

Use training cases to build examples. Use development cases to choose among prompts. Save the test for the frozen choice. Here two training requests ask about the same approval in different words. They belong to one policy family.

Look at the request arriving at the test file. Its request number is new. Its approval number already appears in training. Which file should own this paraphrase if the test measures transfer to unseen policies?

Keep it in training with its family. A checker can flag a family ID in two splits. Suppose someone assigned different family IDs to two wordings of the very same policy. The check could pass. Inspect the underlying policies too.

title: Make a copy with two examples

beats.say: The request is a rollback. In this example a local model double proposes a route and a record ID. The host checks both against the approval. A field description tells the model what to return. Chain of Thought adds a reasoning field.
This one says the approval covers the rollback. You can check that claim against the record too.

Start with an empty student. Labeled Few Shot copies training labels straight into a new program. The copy gets two demonstrations, one rollback and one abstention. The original student keeps zero. This step copies the labels as supplied.
It makes no model calls and never scores either example. For the next experiment, the teacher can be a copy of the student using its configured model.

Try another way to fill the example slots. Let a teacher answer the training questions and record its steps. On the rollback, it answers serve with the approved record. Both fields match. At a threshold of one, this trace passes.
The accepted trace can become a few-shot demonstration in the compiled program. Look at the copied predictor step. It still names the rollback and its approval.
Now ask the teacher about deploying payment-service. It gives the same reply. The reviewed label is abstain with an empty ID. Which of the two traces will the compiled prompt keep?

Only the rollback stays. The deployment scores zero, so its trace is discarded. Two teacher replies left one bootstrapped example. The original student still has zero. Now imagine a two-step teacher whose final answer is right by chance. Check each recorded step before you teach another predictor to repeat it.

title: What does the teacher’s score cover?

beats.say: Look inside a two-step teacher. Its first step says the approval covers deployment. Its final reply happens to abstain with an empty ID. A grader that checks just the final pair gives it one. The unsupported first step can now enter a demonstration too.

Review it against the policy. Collection can stop when the example slots fill, even if training cases remain. What if the grader returns a fraction? In this version, a zero or missing threshold tests the score’s truth value.
A partial score of zero point five, a negative number and NaN are truthy.

Try a separate probe. Give both traces half a point, including the bad deployment. Use a zero threshold. Both pass. Those examples would enter the prompt. Try a threshold of one. Neither passes. The same scores now fall below the threshold. Remove the metric altogether and successful teacher executions pass unchecked.
Choose a threshold and a metric that actually catches the error.

You can search different parts of this program with the same model weights. Bootstrap Random Search tries different subsets of examples. COPRO searches instructions and output prefixes using scores from earlier trials. Its trainset argument supplies development cases.

MIPRO version two searches instructions and examples together across predictors. It proposes instructions from the data and uses Optuna’s Tree-structured Parzen Estimator to choose combinations to try.

GEPA can use a written critique of a recorded run. To point to the bad step, its metric takes five arguments, the label, prediction, trace, predictor name and predictor trace. Adapt our three-argument metric to that interface.

It can return a scalar, or a score and feedback like “check which target the approval names.” The optional program trace serves Flex submodules. The critique proposes a new instruction that still needs evaluation.

title: Which programs and cases will MIPRO try?

beats.say: For a manual MIPRO search, turn off the automatic budget, set the number of candidates, and pass the trial count when you compile. Turn off minibatching so each trial scores the whole validation set. Leave the trial count out and the local check rejects the plan.

The proposer and task predictor can share a model or use separate ones. Want to search instructions alone? Set both demo limits to zero. Start with a student whose slots are empty. Those limits leave existing demos in place. Internal bootstrap examples can still inform the proposals.

Suppose each of two predictors has three instructions to choose from and two possible example sets. Pair each instruction with each set. That gives six choices for the first predictor and six for the second. Pick a column and a row. How many complete programs does the grid hold?
Six times six gives thirty-six programs. Twelve trials can sample just part of that grid. Each candidate’s score is its average across the validation cases.

Give MIPRO ten requests. With no validation set, this version takes roughly the last eighty percent of the list, at least one request and at most a thousand. Here the last eight go to validation. Read requests two and three. Roll back the tests.

Undo the test release. Both use the same approval. Move request three into training with its partner and give MIPRO that split. With minibatching off, each trial scores all seven remaining validation cases. Reserve fresh policies for the final test. If a test case helps you edit the prompt, keep that case for development.

title: Count the work in one search

beats.say: Imagine forty full trials over fifty validation cases. Each little square runs one program on one case. The candidates use two thousand executions. MIPRO also scores the default program across the same fifty cases. That makes two thousand fifty executions. Minibatches and periodic full evaluations would change the count.

Zoom into one square. The first predictor checks the evidence. The second predictor proposes a route. A model-backed judge scores that reply. Trace those three requests back to their one square. With one answer per call, no cache hits and no retries, how many requests cover the full grid?

Six thousand one hundred fifty requests. Teacher and proposal calls are extra. Keep the executions fixed. One cache hit saves one request. The total drops by one. Start again from the uncached total. One extra attempt adds one request. The total rises by one.
The host enforces spend and latency caps. A timed-out request may still incur a charge. Reconcile its outcome. Suppose longer demonstrations add tokens to every request.

Suppose each request carries two thousand five hundred extra logical input tokens, and the system receives one hundred requests per second. That adds two hundred fifty thousand logical input tokens per second. To price it, measure actual input, cached input and output usage by role, then apply the appropriate rates.
Measure first-token latency on the serving system.

title: How many engine calls returned the answers?

beats.say: One more setting changes the request count. DSPy three point four point zero prefers its native engine, L M fifteen, for supported requests. For eligible compatibility cases it selects Lite L L M before inference. An authentication error, timeout or provider failure leaves the selected backend in place. Record which engine handled the call.

Ask the article's local counting engine for two answers to one prompt with caching off. It makes the first call and returns answer one. Only then does the second call begin. It returns answer two. Two sequential engine calls answered one logical prompt.
The pinned native and custom-engine paths work this way. Lite L L M can use a backend’s own multi-answer operation. A provider bill requires that backend’s usage records.

To repeat the comparison, keep the seed, dependencies, model revision, generation settings and cache policy with the data and scorer versions. Record repeated trials. Temperature zero still leaves the backend free to change, and a cached answer may come from an earlier run. Match the effective model and engine to the artifact you evaluated.

title: Would this search fit the request cap?

beats.say: Here’s a smaller plan. Run eight full trials and one baseline over twenty-four cases each. Every execution makes two predictor calls and one judge call. Assume one answer per call, no cache hits and no retries.
Allow twelve teacher requests and nine proposal requests for the whole search. The host allows six hundred fifty requests. Would you start?

Nine passes through twenty-four cases make two hundred sixteen executions. Three calls each give six hundred forty-eight requests. Add twelve for the teacher and nine for proposals. The total reaches six hundred sixty-nine. That exceeds the cap by nineteen.

Try seven trials instead. Keep the baseline and the same overhead. Eight passes now give one hundred ninety-two executions. Removing one pass saves seventy-two requests. The revised plan needs five hundred ninety-seven. It fits. That buys a smaller search. You still have to establish which prompt it chose and how that prompt behaves.

title: Replay the request with a different instruction

beats.say: Return to the deployment request. The baseline instruction says to find an approval and give its ID. It serves with the rollback record. The exact action-and-record metric scores zero. Change just the instruction.
Tell the predictor to match both action and target and to abstain if either lacks support. With the same inputs, which route and record should it return?
The revised prompt abstains with an empty ID. Both fields match, so this worked reply earns one point. A single success is just one case.

Now compare the baseline and Compiled A across twenty development cases. These are illustrative counts. Both programs use the same model weights. The baseline gets fourteen right. Compiled A gets nineteen. Which prompt would you freeze for the test?
Freeze Compiled A. It got five more cases right.
Keep that choice fixed. Both prompts now face twenty cases the search never saw. Does Compiled A keep its lead?

The baseline gets sixteen right. Compiled A gets thirteen. Its five-case lead on development has become a three-case deficit on test. The more prompts we try on those same twenty development cases, the more chances we give the search to pick one that happens to fit their wording. That is selection overfitting. It could explain part of this reversal. Sampling variation or a different mix of policies on test could also change the ranking.

How many test requests did only the baseline get right? The totals do not tell us. Try one possible pairing. Put every one of Compiled A’s thirteen successes under a baseline success. In that arrangement just three cases favor the baseline. Can the same totals hide more disagreement?

Move four of A’s successes onto the four cases the baseline missed. Both totals stay fixed. Now seven cases favor the baseline and four favor A. To learn what actually happened, line up the real answers by request. Check the labels, compare policy families and estimate uncertainty on the paired results. If test feedback changes the prompt, use a fresh test for the new frozen choice.

title: Which parts of the prompt can we save?

beats.say: Return to the program compiled from two labeled examples. Its predictor, called decide, holds the instruction and both examples. Attach model A and save the state as JSON. Suppose we are moving to a service whose default is model B. Which pieces can the file restore on the other side?

The state includes the instruction, both demonstrations, signature metadata and model settings. Supply the matching program class to load it. Check which model the restored predictor will actually use. We can trace that choice on its first request.

title: Where does the first request go?

beats.say: Set the global default to model B, then reload the saved state into the matching class. Both examples come back. Imagine sending the first request from that loaded predictor. Which socket will receive it?

Trace the call through the junction. It reaches model A. Open the predictor settings. The file restored the predictor's own attachment to A, which takes precedence over the global default. Explicitly bind model B with set L M. The next call now goes to B. Evaluate the fixed prompt with that exact model. What else traveled with the file?

The pinned serializer omits the top-level API key. Open the nested configuration. The same serializer preserves the fixture’s nested Authorization header string. Read the demonstrations and instructions too. They can contain sensitive text. Inspect and sanitize the whole saved state before sharing it, then evaluate the approved copy.

Whole-program files use cloudpickle. An untrusted pickle can execute code when loaded. State-only JSON needs compatible reviewed code, dependencies and configuration. Keep the code and artifact digests with the effective model and engine, data and scorer versions, evaluation evidence and a checked rollback target.
A digest identifies the bytes. Record approval separately and retain the approved files.
This approval permits deploying billing-canary. The engineer asks to deploy billing-service. You’re testing the frozen prompt on its intended model. Which route and record should it return?
Abstain, with an empty ID. The action matches, but the targets differ. The candidate served and cited the canary approval. Count that reply as one forbidden serve.

That reply is part of a separate safety sample. All eighty requests in it should get an abstention. The candidate served twice, including the case you just saw. Its mean score improved on development. The release rule allows forbidden serves on at most one percent of these requests. Ship or hold?

Two out of eighty is two and a half percent. Hold this release. Look back at the marked billing request. Inspect both replies against their approvals. If you revise the prompt, freeze it with its model and test on fresh cases. That is the combination to carry into deployment review.
